title: Jeremiah 46:13–28
context: The LORD speaks again to Jeremiah, now about Nebuchadnezzar coming to strike the land of Egypt itself. Egypt's cities are told to prepare, but its strong ones fall because the LORD pushed them, and its foreign soldiers flee. The LORD of Armies swears that the invader will come, and that Egypt, with its gods, Pharaoh, and those who trust in him, will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, though afterward it will be inhabited again. The oracle closes with a word of comfort to Jacob, nearly identical to 30:10–11. Chapters 43–44 also speak of Nebuchadnezzar and Egypt.

verses.text: The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet, how that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon should come and strike the land of Egypt:
verses.arminianNotes: "The word that the LORD spoke to Jeremiah the prophet." Arminian readers see a second oracle about Egypt, now about Nebuchadnezzar invading Egypt's own land rather than defeating its army abroad.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah 43:10 also speaks of the LORD sending Nebuchadnezzar, "my servant," against Egypt. These notes name the connection without harmonizing details.

verses.text: “Declare in Egypt, publish in Migdol, and publish in Memphis and in Tahpanhes; say, ‘Stand up, and prepare, for the sword has devoured around you.’
verses.arminianNotes: "Declare in Egypt, publish in Migdol." Arminian readers see the warning sent to Migdol, Memphis, and Tahpanhes, places where Jews had settled according to 44:1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the cities named are the very places where Judah's refugees had fled for safety. The warning implies that Egypt cannot be a refuge from the LORD's judgment.

verses.text: Why are your strong ones swept away? They didn’t stand, because the LORD pushed them.
verses.arminianNotes: "Why are your strong ones swept away?" Arminian readers see the answer given plainly: "because the LORD pushed them." Egypt's defeat is the LORD's doing, not mere military misfortune.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how directly the verse attributes Egypt's fall to the LORD. Both traditions affirm that God rules over the outcomes of war, while the nations remain responsible for their pride.

verses.text: He made many to stumble. Yes, they fell on one another. They said, ‘Arise! Let’s go again to our own people, and to the land of our birth, from the oppressing sword.’
verses.arminianNotes: "He made many to stumble." Arminian readers see the soldiers falling on one another and deciding to go home, "from the oppressing sword."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that those who say "Let’s go again to our own people" may be foreign troops serving Egypt. Their retreat shows how fragile Egypt's alliances are.

verses.text: They cried there, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise; he has let the appointed time pass by.’
verses.arminianNotes: The fleeing soldiers cry, "Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise." Arminian readers see Pharaoh mocked as all sound and no substance, a ruler who "let the appointed time pass by."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between Pharaoh's reputation and his real power. Judah had looked to Egypt for help, and here Egypt's king is exposed as empty noise.

verses.text: “As I live,” says the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies, “surely like Tabor among the mountains, and like Carmel by the sea, so he will come.
verses.arminianNotes: "As I live," says the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies. Arminian readers see the true King swearing by his own life that the invader will come, as sure as Tabor and Carmel stand out among the hills.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the title "the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies" set against Pharaoh, who is "but a noise." The LORD is the real king over nations.

verses.text: You daughter who dwells in Egypt, furnish yourself to go into captivity; for Memphis will become a desolation, and will be burned up, without inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: "You daughter who dwells in Egypt, furnish yourself to go into captivity." Arminian readers see Egypt told to prepare for exile, as Memphis becomes "a desolation."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal: Egypt, which once held Israel in bondage, now faces captivity. The LORD's justice reaches the empire that seemed secure.

verses.text: “Egypt is a very beautiful heifer; but destruction out of the north has come. It has come.
verses.arminianNotes: "Egypt is a very beautiful heifer." Arminian readers see Egypt pictured as a sleek young cow, beautiful but helpless when "destruction out of the north" comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image combines beauty and vulnerability. Egypt's splendor cannot protect it from the judgment the LORD sends from the north.

verses.text: Also her hired men in the middle of her are like calves of the stall, for they also are turned back. They have fled away together. They didn’t stand, for the day of their calamity has come on them, the time of their visitation.
verses.arminianNotes: "Also her hired men in the middle of her are like calves of the stall." Arminian readers see Egypt's mercenaries, fattened and comfortable, fleeing when "the day of their calamity" comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase "the time of their visitation." The LORD's appointed time of judgment arrives, and no hired strength can stand in it.

verses.text: Its sound will go like the serpent, for they will march with an army, and come against her with axes, as wood cutters.
verses.arminianNotes: "Its sound will go like the serpent." Arminian readers see Egypt reduced to a hissing, retreating snake as the enemy advances "with axes, as wood cutters."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift in images from heifer to serpent to forest. The poetry piles up pictures of Egypt's helplessness before the invading army.

verses.text: They will cut down her forest,” says the LORD, “though it can’t be searched; because they are more than the locusts, and are innumerable.
verses.arminianNotes: "They will cut down her forest," says the LORD. Arminian readers see an invading army so large that it is "more than the locusts," able to cut down even a forest that cannot be searched.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself speaks this verdict. The invader's countless numbers serve the LORD's purpose against Egypt.

verses.text: The daughter of Egypt will be disappointed; she will be delivered into the hand of the people of the north.”
verses.arminianNotes: "The daughter of Egypt will be disappointed." Arminian readers see Egypt's shame as she is "delivered into the hand of the people of the north."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse summarizes the oracle: Egypt's hopes are put to shame. Both traditions treat the LORD's rule over the rise and fall of nations as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt, with her gods and her kings, even Pharaoh, and those who trust in him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: "Behold, I will punish Amon of No, and Pharaoh, and Egypt." Arminian readers see judgment on Egypt's gods, kings, and "those who trust in him."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Amon was an Egyptian god, so the judgment reaches Egypt's religion as well as its rulers. Those in Judah who trusted Pharaoh are warned by implication.

verses.text: I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their lives, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of his servants. Afterwards it will be inhabited, as in the days of old,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: "I will deliver them into the hand of those who seek their lives." Arminian readers see Egypt handed to Nebuchadnezzar, yet with hope: "Afterwards it will be inhabited, as in the days of old."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the promise of later restoration for Egypt. Judgment on the nations is not the LORD's final word. They compare Isaiah 19, which also looks beyond judgment on Egypt.

verses.text: “But don’t you be afraid, Jacob my servant. Don’t be dismayed, Israel; for, behold, I will save you from afar, and your offspring from the land of their captivity. Jacob will return, and will be quiet and at ease. No one will make him afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: "But don’t you be afraid, Jacob my servant." Arminian readers see comfort for God's people after the oracle against Egypt: the LORD will save them "from afar" and bring them home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this promise is nearly identical to 30:10, which reads “Therefore don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant, says the LORD.” These notes name the parallel without merging the two settings.

verses.text: Don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant,” says the LORD, “for I am with you; for I will make a full end of all the nations where I have driven you, but I will not make a full end of you, but I will correct you in measure, and will in no way leave you unpunished.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Don’t be afraid, O Jacob my servant," says the LORD. Arminian readers see both comfort and correction: God will not make a full end of his people, but will "correct you in measure."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 30:11 has almost the same words. The LORD's faithfulness preserves his people even through discipline. Both traditions treat this consolation as shared ground.
